summary:
Same-sex sexual activity, by both men and women, was not criminalized in Burundi before 22 April 2009. Article 567 of the Penal Code, passed on 22 November 2008 and effective on 22 April 2009, punishes sexual relations with a person of the same sex with three months to two years imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 100,000 francs.

Article 29 of the Constitution of Burundi prohibits same-sex marriage. Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not recognized.

United States State Department human rights reports covering 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 document discrimination against gays and lesbians and against LGBT persons under that criminalized framework. The 2015 report records arrests and harassment of LGBT people.

Enforcement has included arrests that ended without conviction. On 1 July 2009 a man in Bujumbura was arrested for being gay, police offered release in exchange for money, and he was released following advocacy. In 2012 two lesbians were briefly arrested and then released. In September 2014 a case in Karuzi Province involving an employee of Viettel and a Burundian man was dropped after three days for lack of evidence.

At least one custodial sentence has combined a homosexuality charge with another offence. On 2 November 2016 the High Court of Cibitoke Province sentenced a 15-year-old boy who admitted rape of a seven-year-old boy to one year in prison on charges of rape of a minor and homosexuality.

In December 2023 President Evariste Ndayishimiye said gay sex is like choosing Satan and that people found in Burundi should be taken to stadiums and be stoned.

In January 2024 President Ndayishimiye repeated the call for homosexuals to be stoned. After the remarks, LGBTQ Burundians reported terror. The Iteka League, operating in exile, described the remarks as a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people. Members of two LGBTQ associations, speaking anonymously, described the remarks as a real license to kill them. Human Rights Watch urged the ruling party to renounce persecution of LGBT people.
tangentialFactors:
The 2015 United States State Department report places the section on violence and discrimination against LGBT persons within a wider crisis marked by extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detention and shutdowns of media.

The 2010 report lists discrimination against gays and lesbians among common abuses alongside killings by security forces, torture and harsh prison conditions.

The 2012 report documents torture, extrajudicial executions and prolonged pretrial detention in the same document that covers discrimination against LGBT persons under the criminalized framework.
localsOnly:
For residents, the constitutional bar and non-recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions precludes formal family status for same-sex couples.

Local organizing operates under constraint. Members of two LGBTQ associations spoke only anonymously after the January 2024 presidential remarks, and the Iteka League cited in that reporting was operating in exile.

The 2009 arrest in Bujumbura involved a police demand for money in exchange for release, with release secured after advocacy, indicating limited access to protection through ordinary enforcement channels for residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
Not sourced in the inventory: rules on legal gender recognition or sex markers, entry or visa rules specific to trans visitors, screening procedures that could disclose trans status, rules on access to facilities, access to gender-affirming care, or hate-crime protection covering gender identity.

Unresolved on the sources cited: whether enforcement practice since the November 2016 sentence in Cibitoke Province has produced further convictions or acquittals, and the current operational status of local LGBTQ associations beyond the anonymous accounts and exile reference from January 2024.

None of the sources cited identifies a decriminalisation measure, exemption or statutory protection for LGBT people.
